chapter_summary:
Docker and Docker Compose are the backbone of any Hyperledger Fabric development environment. Fabric components, from peers to orderers and CAs, run as isolated Docker containers. Docker Compose then orchestrates these containers, allowing you to define and manage your entire Fabric network as a single application. A correct and stable Docker installation is paramount, as almost every subsequent step in setting up your Fabric environment will depend on it.

For **Linux users**, the installation typically involves adding Docker's official GPG key, setting up the stable repository, and then installing `docker-ce` (Community Edition) and `docker-ce-cli`. It's highly recommended to follow the official Docker documentation for your specific Linux distribution (e.g., Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, CentOS) to ensure you get the latest stable version and correct dependencies. After installation, you'll need to start the Docker service (`sudo systemctl start docker`) and enable it to run on boot (`sudo systemctl enable docker`). A crucial step for Linux users is to add your user to the `docker` group. This allows you to run Docker commands without prepending `sudo`, which is not only more convenient but also prevents potential permission issues when Fabric scripts try to interact with Docker. You can do this with `sudo usermod -aG docker $USER`. Remember to log out and log back in (or reboot) for the group changes to take effect. Neglecting this step is a very common source of frustration for new Linux users.

**macOS users** will install Docker Desktop for Mac. This package includes Docker Engine, Docker CLI, Docker Compose, Kubernetes, and an easy-to-use graphical user interface (GUI). The installation is straightforward: download the `.dmg` file from the Docker website, drag the Docker icon to your Applications folder, and then launch Docker Desktop. Once launched, Docker Desktop will start the Docker daemon in the background. You can verify it's running by checking the Docker icon in your menu bar. Docker Desktop handles the complexities of running Docker on macOS, including setting up the necessary virtual machine (VM) if required, making it a relatively smooth experience.

For **Windows users**, Docker Desktop for Windows is also the recommended approach. Similar to macOS, you download the installer from the Docker website. Docker Desktop for Windows requires either WSL 2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux 2) backend or Hyper-V. WSL 2 is generally preferred for better performance and integration. Ensure you have WSL 2 enabled and a Linux distribution installed (e.g., Ubuntu from the Microsoft Store) before installing Docker Desktop. The installer will guide you through the process. After installation, launch Docker Desktop, and it will start the Docker daemon. You'll see the Docker whale icon in your system tray. A common mistake on Windows is not having WSL 2 enabled or not configuring Docker Desktop to use the WSL 2 backend, leading to performance issues or Docker failing to start. Always check the Docker Desktop settings to ensure the correct backend is selected.

Once Docker Engine is installed, you'll need Docker Compose. For Docker Desktop users (macOS and Windows), Docker Compose is typically bundled with the installation, so you often don't need a separate installation step. You can verify this by running `docker-compose --version`. For Linux users, Docker Compose is usually installed separately. The recommended method is to download the Docker Compose binary directly from the official GitHub repository and place it in a directory that's included in your system's PATH, such as `/usr/local/bin`.
```bash
# For Linux: Download Docker Compose binary
sudo curl -L "https://github.com/docker/compose/releases/download/v2.20.2/docker-compose-$(uname -s)-$(uname -m)" -o /usr/local/bin/docker-compose
# Apply executable permissions
sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/docker-compose
# Verify installation
docker-compose --version
```
(Note: Always check the Docker Compose GitHub releases page for the *latest stable version* to replace `v2.20.2` in the `curl` command.)

After installing both Docker and Docker Compose, it's vital to verify their status. Run `docker info` to see detailed information about your Docker daemon, including the number of containers, images, and storage driver. If Docker is not running, this command will fail or show an error. Also, try running a simple container, like `docker run hello-world`, to confirm that Docker can pull an image and execute a container successfully. This "hello-world" test is a quick and effective way to confirm your Docker installation is fully functional before proceeding with Fabric.

screens.title: Installing Docker and Docker Compose
screens.subtitle: Prepare a stable container environment for Hyperledger Fabric

narration.text: Docker Engine and Docker Compose are the foundational pieces you must install correctly before you build or run a Hyperledger Fabric network. In this lesson you'll learn why the Engine matters, how Compose lets you describe an entire Fabric network as a single application, and what to check on Linux, Mac O S, and Windows so containers run reliably. We'll look at the practical steps: installing the engine, installing or confirming Compose, enabling a Linux user to use Docker without elevated permissions, and running a small test container to validate the setup. A working installation removes a common blocker for Fabric lab work and continuous integration. As you watch the visual overview, notice the three key topics you will explore: installing the engine, installing Compose, and verifying and troubleshooting the daemon. A successful hello-world run confirms networking, image pull, and runtime permissions. Keep an eye out for two frequent pitfalls: missing the docker group change on Linux and not enabling WSL 2 or the right backend on Windows. By the end you will be ready to install Docker on your OS, confirm Compose is present, and run a simple container to validate the environment.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Hyperledger Fabric runs as containers. A correct Docker + Compose install prevents most setup failures and saves hours troubleshooting later.

screens.title: What are Docker Engine and Docker Compose?
screens.subtitle: Roles and how they support Hyperledger Fabric

narration.text: Docker Engine is the runtime that executes container images and isolates processes. Docker Compose is a tool that lets you describe and run multi-container applications with a single YAML definition. In the context of Hyperledger Fabric, peers, orderers, and certificate authorities all run as containers under the Engine. Compose then becomes the single point where you define the network topology, environment variables, volumes, and inter-container networking for a Fabric network. A concrete example: a Fabric test network uses Compose to launch two peers, an ordering node, and a CA with one command, ensuring consistent ports, volumes, and environment across machines. A common misconception is thinking Compose itself runs containers; instead, Compose instructs the Engine to start containers according to the YAML. Another pitfall is treating Docker Desktop like only a GUI; it actually bundles Engine, CLI, and Compose so the same CLI commands work in Mac O S and Windows as on Linux. Key takeaway: Engine runs containers; Compose orchestrates sets of containers as a single application definition. How will that change the way you prepare Fabric artifacts and scripts?

keyIdea.title: Engine vs Compose
keyIdea.text: Engine executes; Compose defines and orchestrates multi-container applications such as a Fabric network.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Engine & Compose
Definition

Docker Engine and Docker Compose

Engine executes containers and provides networking and storage. Compose defines multi-container applications so you can start a Fabric network consistently.

Analogy
Think of Engine as the engine in a car and Compose as the blueprint for a fleet of cars working together.
Example
A Fabric test network uses Compose to start peers and an orderer with one command; Engine actually runs each container.
Key takeaway
You will need both: Engine to run containers and Compose to manage multi-container Fabric deployments.
Common misconception
Compose is not a runtime. If Compose fails to start containers, inspect the Engine status and logs; Compose depends on Engine to function.
Quick reference
Engine command
docker run hello-world
Compose command
docker-compose up
Key Takeaway

Compose defines the network; Engine runs it. Confirm both before starting Fabric components.

screens.title: Linux: Installing Docker Engine (apt-based distros)
screens.subtitle: Repository, packages, start and enable the daemon

narration.text: On apt-based Linux distributions the recommended flow is: add Docker's official GPG key, configure the stable repository, install docker-ce and related packages, start the Docker service, and enable it to run on boot. The reason for adding the official repository is to ensure you get supported, up-to-date packages compatible with the Engine. After installation, starting and enabling the service with systemd ensures the daemon is active now and after reboot. A concrete example sequence installs dependencies such as curl and lsb-release, creates the keyrings directory, downloads the GPG key into a keyring, sets the apt source list with the correct architecture and distribution codename, then installs docker-ce packages. A common mistake is omitting the step to enable the service, which leaves the daemon inactive after reboot. Another frequent issue is not installing containerd. io or the compose plugin if you expect bundled Compose functionality. The practical takeaway is to follow the official repository setup for your distribution and confirm the daemon is running before continuing to Fabric setup. Linux: Installing Docker Engine (apt-based distros) means add gpg key, add repository, install packages, start and enable the docker service to keep the daemon running.. In practical terms, repository, packages, start and enable the daemon. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Linux install flow
keyIdea.text: Add GPG key, add repository, install packages, start and enable the Docker service to keep the daemon running.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Linux Installation
Process

Install Docker Engine on apt-based systems

Follow these sequential steps to ensure a stable engine install and avoid missing dependencies.
  1. 1. Update package index and install prerequisites such as curl and ca-certificates.
  2. 2. Add Docker's official GPG key and create /etc/apt/keyrings for the keyring.
  3. 3. Configure the stable repository with the distribution codename and architecture.
  4. 4. Install docker-ce, docker-ce-cli, containerd.io, and optionally Docker Compose plugin.
  5. 5. Start and enable the docker service with systemctl to persist across reboots.
Key Takeaway

Follow the repository setup steps exactly so package versions align with your kernel and container runtime.

Commands (example)
<!-- Example commands shown visually. Adapt for your distro. -->
sudo apt update
sudo apt install ca-certificates curl gnupg lsb-release
sudo mkdir -p /etc/apt/keyrings
curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg
echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg] https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu $(lsb_release -cs) stable" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null
sudo apt update
sudo apt install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin
sudo systemctl start docker
sudo systemctl enable docker
Misconception
Skipping the enable step leaves the daemon inactive after a reboot. Start and enable make the service persistent.

screens.title: Installing Docker Compose on Linux (binary)
screens.subtitle: Download, install, make executable, and verify

narration.text: On many Linux systems Docker Compose is not bundled and must be installed as a standalone binary. The recommended approach is to download the official binary for your kernel and architecture, move it into a directory on your PATH such as /usr/local/bin, and mark it executable. A concrete example from the chapter shows a curl command that fetches a Compose release for the current OS and architecture, then applies executable permissions and verifies the installation with a version check. A frequent mistake is not choosing the latest stable release when you copy the command; always confirm the version string matches a current release. Another issue is placing the binary in a directory not on PATH, which results in the command not being found. The practical verification step is running docker-compose --version and confirming an expected version string. This is a short, repeatable process that ensures your Compose tooling matches what Fabric network definitions expect. Installing Docker Compose on Linux (binary) means download the matching binary, place it in /usr/local/bin, set executable permission, and verify with docker-compose --version.. In practical terms, download, install, make executable, and verify. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Compose binary install
keyIdea.text: Download the matching binary, place it in /usr/local/bin, set executable permission, and verify with docker-compose --version.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Compose on Linux
Walkthrough

Download and install Docker Compose binary

Use the official release matching your OS and architecture. Place the binary in a PATH directory and set executable permissions.

Common pitfall
Forgetting to mark the file executable or placing it outside a PATH causes "command not found" errors even after download.
Key Takeaway

Always verify docker-compose --version after installing the binary to confirm it is executable and on PATH.

Commands (example)
sudo curl -L "https://github.com/docker/compose/releases/download/v2.20.2/docker-compose-$(uname -s)-$(uname -m)" -o /usr/local/bin/docker-compose
sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/docker-compose
# Verify
docker-compose --version
Example explanation
The curl command downloads the correct binary for the kernel and CPU, chmod makes it executable, and the version check confirms success.

screens.title: Configure Docker to run without sudo on Linux
screens.subtitle: Add your user to the docker group and apply changes

narration.text: Running Docker commands with sudo is functional but cumbersome and can cause permission problems when Fabric scripts expect a non-root user. The recommended fix is to add your user to the docker group so Docker sockets can be accessed without elevated privileges. The process is straightforward: run the command to add your user to the docker group, then log out and log back in or reboot so the group membership takes effect. A concrete example is using a command that appends your user to the docker group and then verifying by running docker ps without sudo. A common mistake is skipping the logout step and immediately expecting new permissions to apply, which leads to continued permission denied errors. Another misunderstanding is thinking adding a user to the docker group is equivalent to giving that user full root privileges; while it does grant control over Docker, it specifically allows access to the Docker socket, which can be used to access host resources. The practical takeaway: add your user to the docker group, then restart your session before attempting Fabric commands without sudo.

keyIdea.title: Why add user to docker group
keyIdea.text: It enables running Docker CLI without sudo and prevents permission-related failures during Fabric operations; log out and back in for changes to apply.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Docker Group
Definition

Add your user to the docker group

Grant your user permission to access the Docker socket and run CLI commands without sudo for smoother development workflows.

Why it matters: Fabric scripts often execute Docker commands. If those scripts assume non-root access, missing group membership causes permission denied errors and failed automation.
Caution

Adding a user to the docker group grants control over containers and can affect host security; apply this in trusted environments.

Command (example)
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
# Then log out and log back in, or reboot. After that:
docker run hello-world
Misconception
Expecting immediate effect without logging out is the most common source of frustration. Group membership is applied at session start.

screens.title: Docker Desktop on macOS vs Windows
screens.subtitle: Bundled tools, backends, and common platform issues

narration.text: Docker Desktop for Mac O S and Windows packages Docker Engine, CLI, Compose, and optional Kubernetes in a single installer, simplifying setup compared to Linux. On Mac O S, the installer handles the VM or virtualization layer transparently, so you generally just drag the app to Applications, launch it, and confirm the whale icon shows the daemon is running. On Windows, Docker Desktop supports two backends: WSL 2 and Hyper-V. WSL 2 is typically preferred for better integration and performance; Hyper-V is an alternative when WSL 2 cannot be used. A concrete example: if a Windows user installs Docker Desktop without enabling WSL 2, Docker may fail to start or perform poorly. A frequent troubleshooting step on Windows is checking Docker Desktop settings to ensure the chosen backend is enabled and that a WSL distribution is installed. A common misconception is that Docker Desktop only provides a GUI; it also installs the CLI and Compose so terminal commands behave the same across platforms. The practical tip is to confirm the Docker whale icon indicates a running daemon and to run docker run hello-world to validate the installation regardless of OS.

keyIdea.title: Desktop bundles tools
keyIdea.text: Docker Desktop simplifies setup on macOS and Windows by bundling Engine, CLI, and Compose; ensure the correct backend on Windows for reliable performance.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Desktop Comparison
macOS
Install flow
Download the .dmg, drag Docker to Applications, launch. The Desktop app starts the daemon and bundles Compose.
Verification
Check the whale icon in the menu bar and run docker run hello-world to validate.
Windows
Install flow
Run the Desktop installer. Prefer WSL 2 backend for better performance. Ensure a WSL distribution like Ubuntu is installed.
Common issue
Not enabling WSL 2 or selecting the wrong backend is a frequent cause of Docker Desktop failing to start.
Pro Tip
Regardless of OS, run docker run hello-world and docker-compose --version to confirm both engine and compose are available to the CLI.
No GUI assumptions — validate with the terminal.

screens.title: Verifying your installation
screens.subtitle: docker info, docker run hello-world, and docker-compose checks

narration.text: Verifying Docker installation means confirming the daemon is responsive, images can be pulled, and Compose is available. Start with docker info to get system-wide details such as the number of running containers, images, and the storage driver. If docker info returns an error, the daemon is not running or the CLI cannot reach it. The canonical functional test is docker run hello-world: this command pulls a small test image and executes it; successful output indicates image pull, network, and runtime functionality. For Compose, run docker-compose --version to confirm availability. A concrete example: after installing Engine on Linux, run systemctl status docker to confirm the service is active, then run docker info and finally docker run hello-world. A common misconception is thinking a running Desktop app icon always implies the daemon is healthy; the terminal checks are definitive. Key takeaway: these checks rapidly reveal whether your environment is ready for Fabric, and they are the first troubleshooting steps you should run. Verifying your installation means use docker info and hello-world to confirm daemon health and image pull capability; docker-compose --version confirms compose is available.. In practical terms, docker info, docker run hello-world, and docker-compose checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Verify before you proceed
keyIdea.text: Use docker info and hello-world to confirm daemon health and image pull capability; docker-compose --version confirms Compose is available.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Verification
Terminal checks

Confirm daemon health and Compose availability

# Check daemon and system info
docker info

# Run a small test container to verify pull and run
docker run hello-world

# Verify Compose
docker-compose --version
Interpreting results
  • If docker info returns an error, check systemctl status docker or the Desktop logs to find why the daemon is not reachable.
  • Successful hello-world output shows the image pulled and the container executed correctly.
  • If docker-compose is missing, install the binary on Linux or confirm Desktop includes it on macOS/Windows.
Example output
A successful hello-world run prints a confirmation message from the test container. Capture that output as proof for the lab.
Check your assumptions

Do not assume a GUI icon equals a fully healthy daemon. Use the CLI checks to be certain.

screens.title: Troubleshooting common installation issues
screens.subtitle: Daemon status, permissions, and backend selection

narration.text: Troubleshooting starts by identifying whether the problem is the daemon, permissions, or backend configuration. If docker info fails, check the Docker daemon status with systemctl on Linux or the Desktop logs on Mac O S/Windows. For permission denied errors when running docker commands on Linux, the primary cause is your user not being in the docker group; the fix is adding the user and restarting the session. On Windows, failures to start are often caused by missing WSL 2 support or disabled Hyper-V; check Docker Desktop settings and ensure the chosen backend is available. A concrete troubleshooting sequence: run docker info, then systemctl status docker or inspect Desktop logs, validate group membership on Linux, and if the problem persists, restart the daemon and check Journal logs for errors. A common misconception is assuming re-install fixes everything; often the issue is a misconfigured backend or missing group membership. The practical takeaway is to follow a diagnostic order: daemon health, permission checks, backend settings, then reinstall as a last resort. Troubleshooting common installation issues means check daemon status first, then permissions, then platform backend settings before attempting reinstallation.. In practical terms, daemon status, permissions, and backend selection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Diagnostic order
keyIdea.text: Check daemon status first, then permissions, then platform backend settings before attempting reinstallation.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Troubleshooting
Diagnostic steps
  1. Run docker info to confirm the CLI can reach the daemon.
  2. Inspect the daemon: systemctl status docker and journalctl -u docker on Linux, or Docker Desktop logs on desktop platforms.
  3. Check permissions: ensure user is in docker group and restart session.
  4. Verify backend: on Windows confirm WSL 2 is enabled or Hyper-V is available and selected.
  5. If errors continue, gather logs and consider reinstalling as a last resort.
Common mistake

Reinstalling without checking backend or permissions wastes time. Always inspect daemon logs first.

Quick commands
systemctl status docker journalctl -u docker --no-pager sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
When to escalate
If logs show kernel or storage driver incompatibilities, seek platform-specific guidance rather than repeating installer steps.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and best practices
screens.subtitle: Avoid group, backend, and service mistakes

narration.text: There are recurring pitfalls that new users encounter when installing Docker and Compose. The most common on Linux is forgetting to add your user to the docker group or failing to restart the session, which leads to permission denied errors. On Windows, failing to enable WSL 2 or selecting the wrong backend in Docker Desktop frequently prevents the daemon from starting. Another common error is assuming Compose is always bundled; on Linux you often need to install the binary or plugin. Best practices include following the distribution-specific official repository instructions, verifying the daemon and Compose with the terminal, and capturing the outputs as evidence. A concrete example: if docker run hello-world fails with a permission error, check group membership; if docker info fails entirely, inspect the systemd status or Desktop logs. Top pitfalls

Best practice

Quick fixes
If permission denied: add user to docker group and restart session. If daemon fails: inspect logs and backend settings before reinstalling.

On Linux, download the Compose binary and place it in /usr/local/bin. On Desktop platforms, confirm Compose is bundled.
